mcqs.question: What lets a client use a Proxy without any change to its own code, compared to using the real object directly?
options: The proxy always returns cached results instead of doing real work
The proxy is faster than the real object at every operation
The proxy runs in a separate process from the client
The proxy implements exactly the same interface as the real object, so calls look identical whether or not a proxy is involved
mcqs.explanation: Interface parity is what makes a proxy transparent to callers — the client's code doesn't know or care whether it's calling the real subject or a proxy. Caching, running in a separate process, and being universally faster are properties some proxies have, not the defining trait of the pattern.

mcqs.question: A LazyImage decodes a file only when .render() is first called, instead of when the object is constructed. What kind of proxy is this?
options: A virtual proxy, since it delays creating/loading an expensive resource until it's actually needed
This isn't a proxy — it's just lazy initialization, unrelated to the Proxy pattern
mcqs.explanation: Delaying expensive work until first real use is the textbook virtual proxy. It's not a protection proxy (no permission check) or remote proxy (no network involved), and lazy initialization behind a shared interface with the real object is exactly what the Proxy pattern names.

mcqs.question: Both a CachingImageLoaderProxy and a CompressedStream decorator hold a reference to an object implementing the same interface they implement. What actually distinguishes them?
options: Proxy decides whether/when a call reaches the real object; Decorator adds a new capability once the call does reach it
Proxy always runs remotely, Decorator always runs locally
There is no real difference — they are the same pattern with different names
Decorator can only wrap one object, Proxy can wrap many
mcqs.explanation: The two patterns share nearly identical structure, so intent is the real distinguisher: Proxy gatekeeps or optimizes access without adding capability, Decorator adds a genuinely new responsibility. Locality and wrap-count aren't the distinguishing factors, and treating them as identical misses why both patterns exist separately.

mcqs.question: A team wraps a slow cross-region service call behind a proxy with the exact same interface as the local version, then loops over it 10,000 times the way they looped over the old local calls. What went wrong?
options: The proxy pattern is inherently broken for remote calls
They should have used a Decorator instead of a Proxy
Interface transparency hid a real change in cost and failure mode — a call that's now slow and can time out is being treated like a cheap, always-succeeding local call
The proxy should have compressed the data before sending it
mcqs.explanation: The proxy did its job — same interface — but interface parity doesn't guarantee the same performance or reliability characteristics, and code written for a cheap local call breaks that assumption at scale. This isn't a Decorator problem, and compression wouldn't fix looping 10,000 times over a network call.
